conceptTag: Convince your boss to fund your idea
readerTitle: Ten minutes to win a yes from your boss
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (지역 배관·난방 서비스 회사 안의 배차팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 상사를 설득하는 일은 아이디어가 좋다는 것을 증명하는 일이 아니다. 상사가 이미 책임지고 있는 문제를 상사가 감당할 수 있는 크기로 풀어 주는 일이다.
misconception: 좋은 아이디어라면 자세한 배경 설명과 큰 숫자만 있으면 승인받는다. 반대에 부딪히면 더 강하게 밀어붙여야 한다.

sources.text: 설명용 가상 사례. 유닛 PPL-08의 개념(상사 관리, 명확한 소통, 스토리텔링, 경청)을 한 장면에 적용

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산을 확인하세요. 헛걸음 90건 × 건당 $150 = 월 $13,500, × 12 = 연 $162,000. 헛걸음을 절반으로 줄이면 연 $81,000 절감 대비 코디네이터 연 $55,000.
3번 카드의 C 선택지($162,000을 '절감액'으로 제시)는 의도적으로 틀린 주장입니다. $162,000은 문제의 전체 비용이지 절감액이 아니라는 피드백이 정확한지 확인하세요.
6주 시범 결과(헛걸음 감소)는 이야기 속 가정이며 실제 연구 결과가 아님을 카드 문구로 분명히 했는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Ten minutes to win a yes from your boss
body: You run dispatch at a regional plumbing and heating company. Last month, technicians made **90 trips** to homes where nobody answered the door. Each wasted trip cost about $150 in time and fuel.
You have an idea to fix it, and Thursday you get ten minutes with Dana, the operations director. Four choices decide how it goes.

image.label: A technician's van parked outside a house with no one home
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 공구 가방을 든 기술자가 닫힌 현관문 앞에 서 있고, 뒤에 작업용 밴. 문 옆 창문은 어둡다. 회사 로고나 실제 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What do you prepare?
body: Your idea: hire a coordinator to call customers the day before and confirm a two-hour arrival window. It costs about $55,000 a year. You have two days to get ready.

options.text: A detailed deck on why customer experience matters
options.feedback: It shows effort, but it argues for something Dana may not be judged on. She'll listen politely and file it under 'nice to have'.

options.text: Find out what Dana is measured on this quarter, and frame the idea in those terms
options.feedback: You learn she's under pressure on cost per job. Now your idea is a cost fix, not a customer-service wish.

options.text: Get three technicians to come and back you up
options.feedback: Support helps, but a crowd can feel like pressure. It also doesn't tell you what Dana needs to hear.

cards.title: How do you open?
body: Say you chose B. Dana's quarter is about cost per job. She sits down, checks her watch and says, "Go ahead."

options.text: Walk through how the problem built up over the past year
options.feedback: The history is true, but Dana has to wait minutes to learn what you want. Busy people stop listening while they guess.

options.text: "I'm asking for a three-month trial of one coordinator. It targets wasted trips, which cost us about $13,500 last month."
options.feedback: The ask and the reason come first. Dana knows what she's deciding and can spend the rest of the meeting testing it.
That's the full cost of the problem, not what the fix would save. If Dana spots the stretch, she'll doubt every number after it.

cards.title: "How do you know this is real?"
body: Say you chose B. Dana leans in, then asks for proof.

options.text: Hand her a spreadsheet of all 90 wasted trips
options.feedback: It's thorough, but she can't read it in ten minutes. The data supports you only if she can see the point quickly.

options.text: Tell one trip: a 40-minute drive, nobody home, a customer who forgot. Then give the monthly total
options.feedback: One vivid case makes the problem real. The number shows it isn't a one-off. Together they stick.

options.text: "Honestly, everyone on the team feels it."
options.feedback: Feelings are easy to dismiss. Dana hears a complaint, not a case she could defend to her own boss.

cards.title: "I can't add headcount this quarter."
body: Say you chose B. Dana nods at the story. Then she gives you the real obstacle.

options.text: Repeat the numbers more firmly. The savings speak for themselves
options.feedback: You're answering a question she didn't ask. Pushing harder makes her defend her 'no' instead of solving with you.

options.text: Ask what the limit is, then offer a smaller test: a current dispatcher makes calls two hours a day for six weeks
options.feedback: The limit is new hires, not spending on the problem. A test with no new hire fits inside her constraint and gives you real data.

options.text: Thank her and say you'll bring it back next year
options.feedback: You keep the relationship, but the problem keeps costing money. And you never learned what a 'yes' would need.

cards.softwareNote: Asking leadership for engineering time works the same way. Tie the feature to the metric they're judged on, and offer a time-boxed experiment with a result you agree on upfront.

cards.title: Say you chose B every time.
body: Dana approves the six-week test on the spot. It costs her no new hire and no budget fight. If wasted trips drop, she has a result to take to her own boss. Your pitch had four moves.

breakdown.label: Ask first
breakdown.detail: What you want and why, in one breath

breakdown.label: Story + number
breakdown.detail: One trip, then the monthly total

breakdown.label: Listen, then shrink
breakdown.detail: A test that fits her limit

cards.callout: You didn't win an argument. You made it easy to say yes.
cards.softwareNote: A product manager asking to fund a new onboarding flow could follow the same four moves: the churn metric leadership tracks, the ask up front, one lost customer's story, and a two-sprint test.

cards.title: Framing is not spin.
body: Speaking to your boss's goals only works if the link is honest. If the idea doesn't really help her goal, say so and make the case on its own terms.

A smaller test has a cost too. Six weeks of calls take a dispatcher away from other work, and the result might be unclear. Agree before you start on what will count as success, such as wasted trips down by a third. Otherwise the test can quietly fizzle out.

image.label: A simple scorecard showing a target agreed before a test
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 화이트보드에 "6-week test"라는 제목과 "Success = wasted trips down 1/3" 목표선이 그려진 막대그래프. 두 사람이 화이트보드 앞에서 고개를 끄덕이는 모습. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Make it easy for your boss to say yes.
body: Each decision used an idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1 · Managing up:** start from what your boss is judged on
**Decision 2 · Clear communication:** lead with the ask and the reason
**Decision 3 · Storytelling:** one concrete case, then the number
**Decision 4 · Listening:** find the real limit and design around it
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write your next request in two sentences, the ask first and then the reason in your boss's terms.
